title: Text and attribution
short: An answer to Marlowe's 'Passionate Shepherd', printed in Englands Helicon (1600) as by 'Ignoto' and ascribed to Ralegh by Walton in 1653.
body: The reply first appeared, unsigned except for 'Ignoto' (Latin, 'unknown'), in Englands Helicon (1600), immediately after Marlowe's song; one stanza had already been printed in The Passionate Pilgrim (1599). Izaak Walton, in The Compleat Angler (1653), has a milkmaid's mother sing 'an answer to it, which was made by Sir Walter Raleigh in his younger days', and this ascription has generally been accepted. Rudick's historical edition largely sidesteps questions of authenticity, printing poems in the form in which they were first attributed to Ralegh, and the attribution here rests chiefly on Walton's late report. The archive's text is from Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (1867).

anchor: Then pretty pleasures might me move
title: If ... Then: the conditional frame
short: The reply opens and closes with impossible conditions: she would accept if the world were always young and lovers always true.
body: The first stanza answers Marlowe's 'An if these pleasures may thee move' with its own condition: if the world and love were young, and every shepherd honest, then his pleasures might persuade her. The final stanza returns to the same structure ('But could youth last ... Then these delights my mind might move'). Since neither condition can be met, the polite conditional is a refusal. The same metre (tetrameter couplets) and refrain wording ('To live with thee, and be thy love') imitate Marlowe closely, so the answer is also a parody.

title: truth in every shepherd's tongue
short: The nymph doubts the honesty of shepherds' speeches: love talk and pastoral poetry are suspected of lying.
body: The line questions the sincerity of the lover and also of pastoral poetry, whose shepherds are often poets in disguise. The nymph implies that the shepherd's promises are rhetoric, an echo of Elizabethan suspicions that poets are liars, which Sidney's Defence of Poesie had answered. The idea recurs at line 11 in 'A honey'd tongue, a heart of gall'. The 'tongue' here anticipates the bodily imagery of tongue and heart later in the poem.

title: Time drives the flocks from field to fold
short: Time, absent from Marlowe's perpetual spring, enters the pastoral world: autumn sends sheep from pasture to pen.
body: A 'fold' is an enclosure where sheep are penned, especially in winter. The line introduces the poem's central argument: the passing of the seasons and of human life, which Marlowe's song excludes. Time is personified as a drover. The alliteration of 'field' and 'fold' gives the line a settled, proverbial ring. Marlowe's shepherds 'feed their flocks' in an eternal present; the reply sets those flocks in motion under the pressure of the year's turning.

anchor: rivers rage, and rocks grow cold
title: rivers rage, and rocks grow cold
short: Marlowe's 'shallow rivers' and the 'rocks' the lovers sat on are turned wintry: floods and cold stone.
body: The line directly answers Marlowe's second stanza ('we will sit upon the rocks ... By shallow rivers'). In winter, rivers flood and the rocks are no place to sit. The nymph's method is to keep the shepherd's images but supply what the pastoral leaves out: weather, time and change. The alliteration on 'r' adds harshness. The verb 'rage' also implies passion out of control, a hint that love too may turn violent or destructive.

title: Philomel
short: Philomela, the nightingale of Ovid's myth, falls silent: Marlowe's singing birds stop with the season.
body: In Ovid's Metamorphoses (book 6), Philomela is raped by her brother-in-law Tereus, who cuts out her tongue; she is later transformed into a bird, in the Latin tradition the nightingale. 'Philomel' became a poetic name for the nightingale, whose song is associated with love and grief. Nightingales stop singing in late summer, so the line means that birdsong ends; but the myth also introduces violence and silencing into the pastoral, a darker reply to the madrigal-singing birds of Marlowe's poem. 'Dumb' means mute.

title: The rest complain of cares to come
short: The other birds lament the hardships of the coming winter; 'complain' is to lament.
body: 'Complain' here means to utter a lament (the 'complaint' was a lyric genre). 'The rest' are the other birds or creatures that remain after the nightingale falls silent. Anticipation of future 'cares' is exactly what Marlowe's song suppresses; the nymph's view looks forward. The phrase reverses the shepherd's promise of 'delights', putting worry about the future where he had placed present pleasure. It is also a reminder that in pastoral tradition the shepherd's life was one of seasonal labour as well as song.

title: wanton fields
short: 'Wanton' means luxuriant and also unrestrained or lascivious: the fertile fields are like a careless young lover.
body: 'Wanton' (OED, wanton, adj.) meant luxuriant or growing profusely, playful, and also lustful or undisciplined. The fields are lush in summer, but the word also hints at the erotic carelessness of the shepherd's proposal. Both kinds of wantonness must give way to winter. The adjective thus prepares the moral turn of the stanza from natural to human seasons: wanton youth must also yield to winter. Shakespeare uses the word in both the botanical and erotic senses.

title: To wayward winter reckoning yields
short: The fields must render up their account to perverse winter, as a debtor pays a reckoning.
body: 'Reckoning' is a financial term, an account or bill to be settled, and 'yields' means both produces and surrenders. The fertile fields must pay their debt to winter. 'Wayward' means perverse, contrary, unpredictable. The line answers Marlowe's 'yields' (l. 4), where landscape yields only pleasure: here it yields to time. Financial metaphors of reckoning were also used of death and the Last Judgement.

anchor: honey'd tongue, a heart of gall
title: A honey'd tongue, a heart of gall
short: Sweet speech and a bitter heart: the shepherd's eloquence may hide bitterness or deceit.
body: Gall, bile, was proverbially bitter and associated with rancour; honey with sweet, persuasive speech. The contrast of a honeyed tongue and a bitter heart is proverbial and biblical in flavour (compare Proverbs 5:3-4, where the strange woman's lips drop as a honeycomb but her end is bitter as wormwood). In the stanza it describes the course of passion: sweet in the beginning, bitter in the end.

title: fancy's spring, but sorrow's fall
short: 'Fancy' is amorous desire or infatuation; its springtime becomes sorrow's autumn ('fall'), with a pun on falling into ruin.
body: 'Fancy' in Elizabethan usage meant love, especially fleeting, imaginative infatuation (OED, fancy, n.). The seasonal pun sets 'spring' against 'fall', autumn, and also suggests a moral or sexual fall. 'Fall' evokes autumn (from 'fall of the leaf'). The line makes the seasonal argument into a moral one: love that begins in pleasure ends in grief. Elizabethan readers would also have recognised the commonplace that love is a springtime folly, a theme the reply shares with much moral verse of the period.

title: Point-by-point rebuttal
short: Stanzas 4-5 list the shepherd's gifts back to him, almost word for word, in order to dismiss them.
body: The reply mirrors Marlowe's catalogue of gifts: gown, slippers ('shoes'), beds of roses, cap, kirtle, posies, belt of straw and ivy buds, coral clasps and amber studs. Repetition with the possessive 'thy' hands each object back to the giver. The method, typical of the Elizabethan answer-poem, turns the original into a target, and the near-quotation makes the nymph's wit depend on intimate knowledge of the poem she rejects.

anchor: Soon break, soon wither, soon forgotten
title: Soon break, soon wither, soon forgotten
short: Triple repetition (anaphora) marks the transience of each gift: things break, flowers wither, gifts are forgotten.
body: The threefold 'soon' is anaphora, repetition at the beginning of successive clauses, and the three verbs can be heard as matching kinds of gift: made objects break, flowers wither, and the whole affair is forgotten. The feminine rhyme 'forgotten/rotten' slows the line and gives it a falling cadence. The line also answers the shepherd's implied promise of permanence: his gifts, like his 'May-morning', belong to a single season.

anchor: In folly ripe, in reason rotten
title: In folly ripe, in reason rotten
short: Ripe in folly, rotten in reason: the gifts, like fruit, are mature only as foolishness and already decayed when judged by reason.
body: The line's parallel antithesis ('folly ripe' / 'reason rotten') uses the image of fruit that ripens and rots. As tokens of folly they are perfect; judged by reason they are already corrupt. It is perhaps the poem's most quoted line, a sententia (moral maxim) in the manner of Elizabethan wisdom literature, and characteristic of the moralising wit associated with Ralegh's poetry.

title: But could youth last, and love still breed
short: The closing condition: if youth lasted and love kept growing, she might accept; 'still' means always.
body: The final stanza returns to the conditional of stanza 1. 'Still' means continually, and 'breed' means increase or flourish, with an echo of the flocks' breeding. The condition is impossible, which is the point, but the tone remains wistful: the nymph does not despise pleasure, only its impermanence. Some critics read the poem as a carpe diem argument turned inside out: the passage of time, usually a reason to seize the day, here becomes a reason to refuse.

title: date ... need
short: 'Date' means a term or limit (an expiry date); 'need' means want or necessity: if joys did not end and old age were not needy.
body: 'Date' (OED, date, n.2) in Elizabethan English often meant the limit or end of a period, the term of duration, as in 'death's dateless night' in Shakespeare's Sonnet 30. 'Need' is poverty or want, the hardships of old age. Together they summarise the nymph's argument: pleasures end and old age requires provision. The vocabulary of terms and needs continues the financial metaphor of 'reckoning'.
